title: Drum styles of the era: Walter Johnson and Cozy Cole
summary: Asked about stylistic differences, Moore praises Walter Johnson's hi-hat work with Fletcher Henderson and Cozy Cole's tom-tom playing.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Because I was kind of young and wild, and just (?) about no drum solos. I'd take sometimes three or four choruses on drums, tom-tom, cymbals, snare drum, woodblock -- doing everything. And they wouldn't... They kind of set(?) at me a little bit.

Well, at that time... Now, you had your trio. You're playing in New York. You've had certainly about twenty years of playing experience behind you. And you've had an opportunity to watch and listen to drummers, and you're noting the New Orleans style of drumming, and certainly when you get into the 1930's, there are different styles, different drummers have different tricks that they have, different ways of playing the drums. Did you ever reflect on some of these new drumming styles of that time, some of the things that people were doing that were different from you -- say, like Cozy Cole or Gene Krupa or a young Buddy Rich or Jo Jones -- as far as the style of playing the drums is concerned? Were people looking at you, like Baby Dodds, and saying that they had strong preferences for what you were doing as opposed to a younger drummer, even a drummer who was in twenties, when you were, say, in your thirties...?

Yes, he played with Fletcher Henderson a long time. He was a very good drummer. Smooth. He wasn't a loud drummer. He was a great cymbal man. He used to do a lot of work on the hi-hat cymbal. It was something special. He'd drive the Fletcher Henderson band.
